messages.subject: Mixture of truncated densities
parts:
Hello,

I'll start by stating that I haven't been using Stan for very long so there might be an obvious way to solve my problem, so far I've looked at the relevant examples/sections of Stan's reference manual and haven't been able to find the solution, I apologise if I overlooked it.

Now the model (with some question at the end): I'm trying to fit a mixture of a t-distribution with a normal distribution:

mixture_model_1 <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> N; // sample size
    real x[N]; // observations
    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  }
  parameters {
    simplex[K] theta;
    real mu[K];
    real<lower=0> v;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  model {
    real ps[K];
    mu[1] ~ normal(0, 0.3);
    mu[2] ~ normal(0, 0.3);
    sigma ~ gamma(2, 2);
    for(n in 1:N){      
      ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(x[n], mu[1], sigma);
      ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu[2], 1);
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
  }
'

First I fitted the model to simulated data and I could recover the parameters reasonably well, so that's cool. Here's the R code I used to simulate the data:

set.seed(314)
n.sims <- 25000
x.mix <- sample(1:2, n.sims, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.9, 0.1))
x1 <- rnorm(n.sims, 0, 1)
x2 <- rt(n.sims, 2, 0)
x <- rep(NA, n.sims)
x[x.mix == 1] <- x1[x.mix == 1]
x[x.mix == 2] <- x2[x.mix == 2]

hist(x, breaks = 500)

and the fit call:

mix.data <- list(N = length(x), x = x, K = 2)
fit.mix <- stan(model_code = mixture_model_1, data = mix.data, 
  iter = 1000, chains = 4)

After that I fitted the model to my real data and that worked alright as well, giving meaningful estimates. 

But here comes the problem, the actual model I want to fit is a mixture of a normal distribution centred around 0 and another distribution that has zero density in [-a, a] (where a is a "small" real number), and positive density outside that interval. (I'm trying to fit model 2.6 from this in case you're curious, the zero density restriction correspond to the "zero assumption" in the paper).

I've tried two different models to do so:

-Truncating the t-distributions on both sides

mixture_model_2 <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> N; // sample size
    real x[N]; // observations
    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  }
  parameters {
    simplex[K] theta;
    real mu[K];
    real<lower=0> v;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  model {
    real ps[K];
    mu[1] ~ normal(0, 1);
    mu[2] ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
    for(n in 1:N){      
      ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(x[n], mu[1], sigma);
      // truncate non-null so its 0 in [-a,a]
      ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu[2], 1) - 
        student_t_cdf_log(-2, v, mu[2], 1) - 
        student_t_ccdf_log(2, v, mu[2], 1);
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
  }
'

-Fitting a three component mixture having: one normal distribution in the centre and  2 t-truncated distributions, one for each tail.

mixture_model_3 <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> N; // sample size
    real x[N]; // observations
    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  }
  parameters {
    simplex[K] theta;
    real mu[K];
    real<lower=0> v;
    real<lower=0> v_1;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  model {
    real ps[K];
    sigma ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
    for(n in 1:N){      
      ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(x[n], mu[1], sigma);
      // truncate non-null so its 0 in [-a,a]
      ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu[2], 1) - 
        student_t_cdf_log(-2, v, mu[2], 1);
      ps[3] <- log(theta[3]) + student_t_log(x[n], v_1, mu[3], 1) - 
        student_t_ccdf_log(2, v_1, mu[3], 1);
        
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
  }
'

Unfortunately each model is slower than the other (I actually don't know which one is slower since I haven't waited for them to finish the 1000 samples, they were taking a very very long time). So my questions are:

-Am I using the truncated distributions in the correct way? (I'm guessing that's not the case...)
-What is the correct way to specify such a model in Stan?
-Is fitting the model incorporating the zero assumption fundamentally harder (in some sense) than fitting the one without that assumption? I was expecting that there would be a slow down in the sampling, but perhaps not of several orders of magnitude (which is how it's looking at the moment).

On Aug 1, 2014, at 11:20 AM, Arturo Sánchez Correa <arturo.san...@gmail.com> wrote:

It's easy to overlook things in a manual as big as ours. And
it'll only get bigger as we add more models. But I hope we can
organize the principles better in the future so they're not all
buried in with the models.

> Now the model (with some question at the end): I'm trying to fit a mixture of a t-distribution with a normal distribution:
>
> mixture_model_1 <- '
> data {
> int<lower=0> N; // sample size
> real x[N]; // observations
> int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
> }
> parameters {
> simplex[K] theta;
> real mu[K];
> real<lower=0> v;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
> model {
> real ps[K];
> mu[1] ~ normal(0, 0.3);
> mu[2] ~ normal(0, 0.3);
> sigma ~ gamma(2, 2);
> for(n in 1:N){
> ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(x[n], mu[1], sigma);
> ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu[2], 1);
> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
> }
> }
> '

You wouldn't want to use a simplex for a two-component mixture.
It's easier and a bit more arithmetically stable to use

real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;

log(theta) + normal...

log1m(theta) + student_t

It also makes it easier to put a prior on theta or otherwise
constrain it. But if you are going to generalize to more components,
then you need this.

Also there's a two-argument log_sum_exp() which will be more
efficient than using an array.

So I'd write the loop as:

for (n in 1:N)
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta) + normal...,
log1m(theta) + student_t...));

> for(n in 1:N)

>
> First I fitted the model to simulated data and I could recover the parameters reasonably well, so that's cool. Here's the R code I used to simulate the data:
>
> set.seed(314)
> n.sims <- 25000
> x.mix <- sample(1:2, n.sims, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.9, 0.1))

> x2 <- rt(n.sims, 2, 0)

You might want to print with more digits. You probably don't need
600 effective samples in an appliation --- this is indeed sampling
very efficiently (3 iterations or so per effective sample).

> After that I fitted the model to my real data and that worked alright as well, giving meaningful estimates.
>
> But here comes the problem, the actual model I want to fit is a mixture of a normal distribution centred around 0 and another distribution that has zero density in [-a, a] (where a is a "small" real number), and positive density outside that interval. (I'm trying to fit model 2.6 from this in case you're curious, the zero density restriction correspond to the "zero assumption" in the paper).

Presumably not with empirical Bayes, though, right? We can
just fit the whole model in Stan.

> I've tried two different models to do so:
>
> -Truncating the t-distributions on both sides
>
> mixture_model_2 <- '
> data {
> int<lower=0> N; // sample size
> real x[N]; // observations
> int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
> }
> parameters {
> simplex[K] theta;
> real mu[K];
> real<lower=0> v;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
> model {
> real ps[K];
> mu[1] ~ normal(0, 1);
> mu[2] ~ normal(0, 1);
> sigma ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
> for(n in 1:N){
> ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(x[n], mu[1], sigma);
> // truncate non-null so its 0 in [-a,a]
> ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu[2], 1) -
> student_t_cdf_log(-2, v, mu[2], 1) -
> student_t_ccdf_log(2, v, mu[2], 1);
> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
> }
> }
> '

student_t(...)
log ----------------
cdf(high) - cdf(low)

should be

log student_t - log (cdf(high) - cdf(low))

The CDFs can't be done outside the log here, unless I'm missing some
trick of arithmetic.

The real problem with this model is that it's not differentiable at the
points -a or a, which messes up the guarantees of HMC.

Also, I'm not sure our increment_log_prob does the right thing with
-infinite values of one of the arguments. Probably not because of the
gradients. It'd be better to do this:

if (x[n] < -a || x[n] > a) {
increment_log_prob(...student_t...)
} else {
mixture with log_sum_exp
}

It doesn't solve the non-differentiability problem, though.

Is there any way to make this model smoother? Andrew may want to
jump in on why he doesn't like this kind of model.

>
> -Fitting a three component mixture having: one normal distribution in the centre and 2 t-truncated distributions, one for each tail.
>
> mixture_model_3 <- '
> data {
> int<lower=0> N; // sample size
> real x[N]; // observations
> int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
> }
> parameters {
> simplex[K] theta;
> real mu[K];
> real<lower=0> v;
> real<lower=0> v_1;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
> model {
> real ps[K];
> sigma ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
> for(n in 1:N){
> ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(x[n], mu[1], sigma);
> // truncate non-null so its 0 in [-a,a]
> ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu[2], 1) -
> student_t_cdf_log(-2, v, mu[2], 1);
> ps[3] <- log(theta[3]) + student_t_log(x[n], v_1, mu[3], 1) -
> student_t_ccdf_log(2, v_1, mu[3], 1);
>
> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
> }
> }
> '
Again, you'd want to use conditionals here if you can't reformulate the model.

>
> Unfortunately each model is slower than the other (I actually don't know which one is slower since I haven't waited for them to finish the 1000 samples, they were taking a very very long time).

My advice would be to never start with so many samples it doesn't finish.
Run 10 samples or 20 samples just to see if there are problems.

> So my questions are:
>
> -Am I using the truncated distributions in the correct way? (I'm guessing that's not the case...)
See above.
> -What is the correct way to specify such a model in Stan?
See above, but I'd recommend reformulating it.

> -Is fitting the model incorporating the zero assumption fundamentally harder (in some sense) than fitting the one without that assumption? I was expecting that there would be a slow down in the sampling, but perhaps not of several orders of magnitude (which is how it's looking at the moment).

Yes. The real problem though, in your slowdown, is the infinities
which you can get rid of with conditionals.

And thanks for giving us the whole model and background --- it makes it
so much easier to comment.

- Bob

Thanks for the help Bob, your input was extremely useful! Adding the conditional statement to avoid the INFs going to increment_log_prob fixed the massive slow down.

I'll post the updated model here for future reference.

mixture_model <- '

data {
    int<lower=0> N; // sample size
    real x[N]; // observations

real a; // parameter of the zero assumption
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=1> theta; 
    real mu_1;
    //real mu_2;

real<lower=0> v;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  model {

real ps[2];    
    mu_1 ~ normal(0, 1);
    //mu_2 ~ normal(0, 1);
    v ~ gamma(4, 2); // mean 2, variance 1
    sigma ~ gamma(1, 1); // mean 1, variance 1

    for(n in 1:N){      
      ps[1] <- log(theta) + normal_log(x[n], mu_1, sigma);

      if(x[n] < -a || x[n] > a){

        ps[2] <- log1m(theta) + student_t_log(x[n], v, 0, 1) - 
          student_t_cdf_log(-a, v, 0, 1) - log(2); 
      
        // - log(2) to normalise accounting for both tails
        // this assumes that mu_2 is close to 0 
        // it is exact when mu_2 = 0 
        
        // ps[2] <- log1m(theta) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu_2, 1) - 
        //   student_t_cdf_log(-a, v, mu_2, 1) - log(2); 
      
        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));  

      } else {
        increment_log_prob(ps[1]);
      }
    }
  }
'

Fitting it to simulated data with:

set.seed(314)
n <- 25000
x.mix <- sample(1:2, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.9, 0.1))
x.1 <- rnorm(n)
x.2 <- rt(n, 2)
a <- 2
n.A <- sum(x.2 < a & x.2 > -a)
while(n.A > 0){
  # print(n.A)
  x.2[x.2 <= a & x.2 >= -a] <- rt(n.A, 2)
  n.A <- sum(x.2 <= a & x.2 >= -a)
}
x <- rep(NA, n)
x[x.mix == 1] <- x.1[x.mix == 1]
x[x.mix == 2] <- x.2[x.mix == 2]

As for the comments in your reply:
-Yep, I fitted the full bayes model, not the empirical bayes.
-On the particular model choice: I first thought of fitting a single t distribution to the data and just use that, I fitted that and did not get great results. Then I looked at the p-values under the N(0,1) null:

On Friday, 1 August 2014 16:20:53 UTC+1, Arturo Sánchez Correa wrote:

Hello,

I'll start by stating that I haven't been using Stan for very long so there might be an obvious way to solve my problem, so far I've looked at the relevant examples/sections of Stan's reference manual and haven't been able to find the solution, I apologise if I overlooked it.

Now the model (with some question at the end): I'm trying to fit a mixture of a t-distribution with a normal distribution:

mixture_model_1 <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> N; // sample size
    real x[N]; // observations
    int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  }
  parameters {
    simplex[K] theta;
    real mu[K];
    real<lower=0> v;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  model {
    real ps[K];
    mu[1] ~ normal(0, 0.3);
    mu[2] ~ normal(0, 0.3);
    sigma ~ gamma(2, 2);
    for(n in 1:N){      
      ps[1] <- log(theta[1]) + normal_log(x[n], mu[1], sigma);
      ps[2] <- log(theta[2]) + student_t_log(x[n], v, mu[2], 1);
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
  }
'

First I fitted the model to simulated data and I could recover the parameters reasonably well, so that's cool. Here's the R code I used to simulate the data:

set.seed(314)
n.sims <- 25000

After that I fitted the model to my real data and that worked alright as well, giving meaningful estimates. 

But here comes the problem, the actual model I want to fit is a mixture of a normal distribution centred around 0 and another distribution that has zero density in [-a, a] (where a is a "small" real number), and positive density outside that interval. (I'm trying to fit model 2.6 from this in case you're curious, the zero density restriction correspond to the "zero assumption" in the paper).

I've tried two different models to do so:
